title: Qantas 72

agencies.name: Australian Transport Safety Bureau
agencies.report_title: In-flight upset, Airbus A330-303, VH-QPA, 154 km west of Learmonth, WA, 7 October 2008

location.name: Indian Ocean, 154 km west of Learmonth, Western Australia

summary: Cruising at 37,000 ft off Western Australia, the A330's number 1 air data inertial reference unit began outputting intermittent spikes on many parameters. The autopilot disconnected and a stream of spurious warnings followed. Two minutes later the flight control computers, acting on spike angle-of-attack values, commanded an abrupt nose-down pitch that threw unrestrained occupants against the ceiling; a second, smaller pitch-down followed. The crew diverted to Learmonth, where the aircraft landed safely; 12 people were seriously injured and many more hurt.
probable_cause: The ATSB found that one of the aircraft's three ADIRUs entered a failure mode in which it output numerous spikes with incorrect data and labels, including angle-of-attack spikes. A limitation in the flight control primary computers' algorithm for processing angle-of-attack data meant that two spikes 1.2 seconds apart could pass the filtering and trigger the high-AoA protection, commanding the pitch-downs. The ADIRU failure mode's origin could not be determined; the FCPC algorithm limitation had not been identified during the design and certification safety assessment.

factors.evidence: ADIRU 1 began outputting spikes in many parameters with incorrect data and labels at 0440:28 UTC; the specific trigger for the failure mode could not be identified.
Autopilot 1 disconnected at the onset of the ADIRU failure, and the crew flew manually with numerous alerts active.
Spurious overspeed and stall warnings alternated on the flight deck as a result of the corrupted air data.
The crew received a large number of spurious warnings, cautions and fault messages that did not reflect the actual aircraft state, and no procedure existed for the ADIRU failure mode.

The FCPC angle-of-attack processing algorithm could not correctly manage a scenario with multiple spikes 1.2 seconds apart, so the spikes triggered the high-AoA protection and the pitch-down commands.
The ATSB found that the ADIRU failure mode and the FCPC algorithm's vulnerability to it were not identified in the design and certification safety assessment process.
The two pitch-down manoeuvres were commanded by the flight control system, not the crew; the first reached about -0.8 g and 8.4 degrees nose-down.
The crew dealt with continuous alerts, cabin injuries and a diversion with degraded information.
After declaring PAN and then MAYDAY, the crew landed at Learmonth about 50 minutes after the upset.

events.text: Cruising at FL370 toward Perth with 303 passengers and 12 crew; the captain is pilot flying and the first officer is on a rest break, with the second officer in the right seat.
ADIRU 1 begins outputting intermittent spikes on multiple parameters with incorrect labels; autopilot 1 disconnects and a NAV IR 1 FAULT is displayed with a master caution.
Stall and overspeed warnings alternate, and numerous spurious ECAM cautions appear; the captain's airspeed and altitude indications show momentary spikes.
The captain flies manually and the crew begin assessing the alerts; the first officer is recalled to the flight deck.

The flight control computers, acting on two angle-of-attack spikes 1.2 s apart, command an abrupt nose-down: about 8.4 degrees pitch-down and -0.8 g. Unrestrained passengers and crew strike the cabin ceiling; the aircraft loses about 650 ft.
The captain applies back-stick and the aircraft returns to about FL370; the crew make a PAN call and begin considering a diversion.
A second, smaller uncommanded pitch-down occurs; the aircraft loses about 400 ft before the crew recover.
The crew decide to divert to Learmonth, the nearest suitable airport, and declare PAN; on learning of serious cabin injuries they upgrade to MAYDAY.
Descent and approach to Learmonth flown manually with the crew treating the flight control and air data indications with caution.
The aircraft lands at Learmonth. Twelve people are seriously injured and many others hurt; ambulances and later aeromedical flights take the injured to Perth.

recommendations.text: Redesign the flight control primary computer angle-of-attack processing algorithm so that erroneous spike data cannot trigger the high angle-of-attack protection, and provide crews with a procedure for the ADIRU failure mode.
recommendations.outcome: Airbus modified the FCPC software (mandated by EASA airworthiness directive) and issued an operations engineering bulletin instructing crews to switch off the affected ADIRU.

recommendations.text: Investigate the ADIRU failure mode and improve the unit's internal data checking and built-in test so that corrupted output is detected and flagged.
recommendations.outcome: The ADIRU's failure mode could not be reproduced; the manufacturer improved the unit's data-integrity checks.

recommendations.text: Reinforce advice to passengers to keep seat belts fastened while seated, since most injuries were to unrestrained occupants.

safety_changes: Airbus redesigned the A330/A340 FCPC angle-of-attack algorithm; the modification was mandated by airworthiness directive.
An operations engineering bulletin and later a permanent procedure instruct crews to switch off an ADIRU displaying the NAV IR fault so that its data is no longer used.
The FAA and EASA issued airworthiness directives on the affected Northrop Grumman ADIRU model.
The ATSB issued safety advice on the importance of keeping seat belts fastened when seated.

notes: Clock times for the ADIRU failure (0440:28), first pitch-down (0442:27) and second pitch-down (0445:08) are as recalled from the ATSB report; the landing time (0532) is approximate.
Location latitude and longitude are an approximation of 154 km west of Learmonth over the Indian Ocean.
The report describes a subsequent reversion of the flight control law; this is omitted because the exact circumstances were not verified.
Serious injuries are given as 12 (one flight attendant and 11 passengers); over 100 occupants received some injury.
